title: Arrow, Parquet, and DuckDB for Marketing Analytics
text:
This site is a companion resource for the Marketing Analytics course at Cal Poly Pomona MSDM Program. It provides a hands-on, code-first introduction to modern tools for working with large-scale marketing data in R — specifically the kind of high-volume event data that real-world analytics platforms like Google Analytics 4 produce.
All examples use the GA4 Obfuscated Sample E-commerce Dataset — a publicly available BigQuery dataset derived from real user behavior on the Google Merchandise Store. This means every technique you learn here applies directly to the GA4 data your future employer is already collecting.

title: Arrow, Parquet, and DuckDB for Marketing Analytics
text:
Why These Tools?
Traditional approaches to marketing data analysis load everything into RAM as a flat data frame. This works fine for small datasets but breaks down quickly when you have millions of events, dozens of dimensions, and deeply nested data structures. The tools in this series solve each layer of that problem:






NoteParquet



Stores data in a compressed columnar format that is 10–50× smaller than CSV and reads 5–10× faster. It is the industry standard for analytical data storage and is readable by R, Python, Spark, and Tableau.








NoteArrow



A library for reading, writing, and processing Parquet files in R. It allows you to query files that are larger than your RAM by loading only the columns and rows your query actually needs — a technique called lazy evaluation.








NoteDuckDB



An embedded analytical database that runs inside R with zero server setup. It reads Parquet files directly and executes SQL or dplyr queries at speeds that rival dedicated cloud data warehouses.








Noteduckplyr



Brings DuckDB’s engine to your existing dplyr code with no syntax changes — the same verbs, the same pipes, dramatically faster execution on large data. The ideal upgrade path from dplyr for production-scale marketing analysis.

text:
3.1 duckplyr vs dplyr


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
# ── What changes: ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#   library(dplyr)    →   library(duckplyr)
#   That's it. Seriously.

# ── What stays the same: ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#   All verb names: filter, select, mutate, group_by, summarise,
#                   arrange, join, slice, rename, distinct...
#   All syntax: pipes, quasiquotation, across(), where()...
#   All output: tibbles, same column names, same data types

# ── What is different under the hood: ─────────────────────────────────────────
#   dplyr    executes in R's vector engine
#   duckplyr executes in DuckDB's columnar engine

# ── Performance difference: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# For small data (< 100k rows): negligible, sometimes dplyr is faster
# For large data (> 1M rows):   duckplyr is 10-100x faster
# For larger-than-RAM data:     dplyr fails, duckplyr works
```

3.2 duckplyr vs DuckDB + dbplyr


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
# ── DuckDB + dbplyr requires: ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. Create a connection object
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), "data/ga4.duckdb")
# 2. Create table references
events <- tbl(con, "ga4_events")
# 3. Write your query
result <- events |>
  filter(...) |>
  summarise(...) |>
  # 4. Explicitly collect results
  collect()
# 5. Remember to disconnect
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

# ── duckplyr requires: ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 1. Load the library
library(duckplyr)
# 2. Write your query (same as dplyr)
result <- ga4_events |> filter(...) |> summarise(...)
# That's it — no connection, no collect(), no disconnect

# ── The translation gap: ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# dbplyr TRANSLATES dplyr to SQL — some verbs have no SQL equivalent
# duckplyr REIMPLEMENTS dplyr using DuckDB — much more complete coverage

# Example: dbplyr cannot translate some R functions
tbl(con, "ga4_events") |>
  mutate(path = stringr::str_remove(page_url, "\\?.*$")) |>
  collect()
#> Error: str_remove() is not supported in SQL translation

# duckplyr handles it natively
ga4_events |>
  mutate(path = stringr::str_remove(page_url, "\\?.*$"))
#> Works — DuckDB handles the regex directly
```

text:
3.3 The Fallback System — Why duckplyr Is Safe to Use
This is duckplyr’s most important design feature. When it encounters something it cannot execute in DuckDB, it silently falls back to dplyr rather than throwing an error:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(duckplyr)

# duckplyr executes this in DuckDB (fast path)
result1 <- ga4_events |>
  filter(event_name == "purchase") |>
  group_by(event_date) |>
  summarise(n = n())
# → executed by DuckDB engine ✓

# duckplyr cannot handle this custom R function in DuckDB
my_custom_function <- function(x) paste0("[", x, "]")

result2 <- ga4_events |>
  mutate(labeled = my_custom_function(event_name))
# → falls back to dplyr silently ✓ (no error, correct result)

# You can monitor fallbacks to understand your code
duckplyr::fallback_sitrep()
# Reports which operations fell back and why
```




Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Control fallback behaviour explicitly
options(duckplyr.fallback = "warn") # Warn when falling back
options(duckplyr.fallback = "error") # Error instead of falling back
options(duckplyr.fallback = "ignore") # Silent fallback (default)
```

4.2 Reading Data into duckplyr
duckplyr has native methods for reading Parquet and CSV files directly:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(duckplyr)
library(arrow)

# ── Method 1: From a tibble already in memory ─────────────────────────────────
ga4_tibble <- readRDS("data/ga4_raw.rds")

# Convert tibble to duckplyr frame (enables DuckDB execution)
ga4_duck <- as_duckplyr_df(ga4_tibble)
class(ga4_duck)
#> [1] "duckplyr_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"

# ── Method 2: Read Parquet directly — most powerful approach ──────────────────
# No RAM used — DuckDB streams from disk as needed
ga4_events <- duckplyr::df_from_parquet("data/ga4_flat.parquet")
ga4_params <- duckplyr::df_from_parquet("data/ga4_event_params.parquet")
ga4_sessions <- duckplyr::df_from_parquet("data/ga4_sessions.parquet")
ga4_items <- duckplyr::df_from_parquet("data/ga4_items.parquet")

# Each of these is a duckplyr_df — a lazy reference to the Parquet file
# Nothing is loaded into RAM until you need actual values
class(ga4_events)
#> [1] "duckplyr_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"

# ── Method 3: Read multiple Parquet files with wildcard ───────────────────────
# Perfect for GA4's one-file-per-day pattern
ga4_all_days <- duckplyr::df_from_parquet("data/ga4_day_*.parquet")

# ── Method 4: From Arrow dataset ──────────────────────────────────────────────
ga4_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")
ga4_duck <- as_duckplyr_df(ga4_arrow)
```

5.4 Analysis 3: Page Performance from event_params


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

# ── Work directly with the long-format params table ───────────────────────────
# duckplyr reads the Parquet file and filters on disk — no RAM spike

top_pages <- ga4_params |>
  filter(
    event_name == "page_view",
    key == "page_location",
    !is.na(param_value)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Parse URL path — duckplyr passes regex to DuckDB
    page_path = str_remove(param_value, "^https?://[^/]+"),
    page_path = str_remove(page_path, "\\?.*$"),
    page_path = str_remove(page_path, "#.*$"),
    page_path = if_else(page_path == "" | is.na(page_path), "/", page_path),
    # Categorise by section
    section = case_when(
      page_path == "/" ~ "Home",
      str_detect(page_path, "^/google\\+re|/store") ~ "Store",
      str_detect(page_path, "^/product") ~ "Products",
      str_detect(page_path, "^/basket|/cart") ~ "Cart",
      str_detect(page_path, "^/checkout") ~ "Checkout",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(section, page_path) |>
  summarise(
    page_views = n(),
    unique_users = n_distinct(user_pseudo_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(page_views)) |>
  slice_head(n = 20)

# Visualise
top_pages |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  mutate(
    page_path = str_trunc(page_path, 40),
    page_path = fct_reorder(page_path, page_views)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = page_path, y = page_views, fill = section)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = comma(page_views)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Section") +
  labs(
    title = "Top 15 Pages by Page Views",
    subtitle = "Computed via duckplyr on Parquet — no full load into RAM",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Page Views"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

5.5 Analysis 4: Purchase Funnel


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

# ── Funnel stages ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
funnel_stages <- c(
  "view_item",
  "add_to_cart",
  "begin_checkout",
  "add_payment_info",
  "purchase"
)

funnel_labels <- c(
  "view_item" = "View Item",
  "add_to_cart" = "Add to Cart",
  "begin_checkout" = "Begin Checkout",
  "add_payment_info" = "Add Payment",
  "purchase" = "Purchase"
)

# ── Count users at each stage using duckplyr ──────────────────────────────────
funnel_data <- ga4_events |>
  filter(event_name %in% funnel_stages) |>
  group_by(event_name) |>
  summarise(
    users = n_distinct(user_pseudo_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    stage_label = recode(event_name, !!!funnel_labels),
    stage_order = match(event_name, funnel_stages)
  ) |>
  arrange(stage_order) |>
  mutate(
    pct_of_top = users / max(users),
    pct_prev = users / lag(users),
    drop_off = 1 - pct_prev
  )

# ── Visualise ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
funnel_data |>
  mutate(stage_label = fct_inorder(stage_label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stage_label, y = users, fill = pct_of_top)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = glue("{comma(users)}\n{percent(pct_of_top, accuracy=0.1)}")),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.8,
    lineheight = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = funnel_data |> filter(!is.na(drop_off)),
    aes(
      x = stage_order - 0.5,
      y = max(funnel_data$users) * 0.6,
      label = glue("▼{percent(drop_off, accuracy=1)}")
    ),
    colour = "#e53935",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#bbdefb", high = "#1565c0") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Purchase Funnel",
    subtitle = "duckplyr: DuckDB engine, dplyr syntax",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Unique Users"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11))
```

```{r}
# ── Daily revenue with 7-day rolling average ──────────────────────────────────
```

1.1 What is Apache Arrow?

Apache Arrow is a language-agnostic software framework for developing data analytics applications that process columnar data. It contains a standardized column-oriented memory format that is able to represent flat and hierarchical data for efficient analytic operations on modern CPU and GPU hardware (https://en.wikipedia.org/).
Arrow can be used with Apache Parquet, Apache Spark, NumPy, PySpark, pandas and other data processing libraries. The project includes native software libraries written in C, C++, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Julia, MATLAB, Python (PyArrow[8]), R, Ruby, and Rust. Arrow allows for zero-copy reads and fast data access and interchange without serialization overhead between these languages and systems (https://en.wikipedia.org/).

1.3 What you will learn from this lecture

You’ll learn about a powerful alternative: the parquet format, an open standards-based format widely used by big data systems.
parquet is designed for efficient storage and fast querying, making it ideal for large datasets. It’s a columnar storage format, which means it stores data by columns rather than rows, allowing for better compression and faster read times.
We’ll pair parquet files with Apache Arrow, a cross-language development platform for in-memory data.
We’ll use Apache Arrow via the arrow package, which provides a dplyr backend allowing you to analyze larger-than-memory datasets using familiar dplyr syntax.
Both arrow and dbplyr provide dplyr backends, so you might wonder when to use each.

1.4 When to Use Arrow vs. dbplyr

Use arrow when working with large datasets stored in parquet files, especially when you want to perform in-memory analytics without the overhead of a database connection.
Use dbplyr when you have data stored in a relational database and want to leverage SQL for querying, especially if you need to perform complex joins or transactions that are better handled by a database system.

4.1 collect() vs. compute()
collect()

Executes the query and pulls the result into R as a local tibble. Now the data lives in your R session’s memory.
Use it as the final step when you’re done filtering/aggregating and need the data for plotting, modeling, or exporting.

5.1 What is Apache Parquet?
Apache Parquet is an open-source columnar storage file format designed for efficient data storage and retrieval, particularly in big data ecosystems.

parquet is used for rectangular data.
It is a custom binary format specifically for the needs of big data.


5.1.1 Key Features

Compression — Similar values stored together compress extremely well (e.g., a column of integers vs. mixed row data). Supports Snappy, Gzip, Zstd, etc.
Predicate pushdown — Stores min/max statistics per row group, so query engines can skip entire chunks of data without reading them.
Schema evolution — Columns can be added or removed over time without rewriting old files.
Nested data support — Handles complex types like arrays, maps, and structs (using Dremel encoding).
Language agnostic — Readable by Python, R, Java, Scala, C++, and more.

1.1 What is DuckDB?
DuckDB is an embedded analytical database engine — think of it as “SQLite, but built for analytics.” It runs entirely inside your R process with no server, no installation, no configuration. You just install the package and it works.
It was designed from the ground up for OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) workloads — the kind of heavy aggregations, joins, and scans that are typical in data analysis, as opposed to transactional row-by-row operations.

SQLite was built for this (transactional — many small reads/writes):

“Insert one customer order”
“Update one user’s address”
“Delete one session record”

DuckDB was built for this (analytical — few large scans):

“What was total revenue by channel across 50 million events?”
“Which pages had the highest bounce rate last quarter?”
“Give me the 99th percentile session duration by device type”

1.2 Three Remarkable Features

1.2.1 1. It Lives Inside R — No Server Needed
Traditional database setup (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake):

Install database server
Configure network/ports
Create users and permissions
Start the server process
Connect from R
Manage the server forever

DuckDB setup:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false         
install.packages("duckdb")
library(duckdb)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())   # That's it. Running in 1 second.
```




1.2.2 2. It Is Shockingly Fast

DuckDB uses columnar storage and vectorised execution — it reads only the columns your query needs and processes thousands of rows simultaneously using modern CPU instructions:

Benchmark: Count events by type across 10 million GA4 rows

data.frame in RAM: ~4.2 seconds
data.table: ~0.8 seconds
dplyr on tibble: ~3.1 seconds
DuckDB on parquet file: ~0.3 seconds ← faster than data in RAM
DuckDB on DuckDB file: ~0.1 seconds



1.2.3 3. It Reads Parquet Directly — Without Loading Into RAM

This is the feature that changes everything for large datasets:

```{r}
# Traditional approach — must fit in RAM
ga4_data <- arrow::read_parquet("data/ga4_events.parquet")  # ~4 GB into RAM
result   <- ga4_data |> filter(...) |> summarise(...)        # then query

# DuckDB approach — reads only what the query needs
con    <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
result <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT event_name, COUNT(*) as n
  FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_events.parquet')
  WHERE event_date >= '2021-01-01'
  GROUP BY event_name
")
# DuckDB scans only the event_name and event_date columns
# Never loads price, device, geo, or any other column into RAM
```

1.3 Why use DuckDB?

It’s fast. DuckDB uses a columnar execution engine with vectorized query processing, meaning it processes chunks of columns at a time rather than row by row. For analytical queries on large data, this is dramatically faster than base R or even many database solutions.
It’s serverless. No Docker, no Postgres instance, no DBA needed. It lives inside your session like any other R package.
It speaks SQL fluently. You can write standard SQL, or use it as a dplyr backend via dbplyr — so you don’t need to learn a new API.
It handles larger-than-memory data. DuckDB can query files that don’t fit in RAM by streaming and processing them in chunks, making it genuinely useful for big data workflows.
It integrates natively with Parquet and Arrow. It can directly query .parquet files on disk without loading them into memory first — no import step needed.

DuckDB is how you query it with full SQL power, with or without loading into memory







Tip



They work beautifully together — DuckDB can read Arrow tables directly and query Parquet files on disk, and you can pass results back to Arrow or collect into R.

2.2 Downloading and Caching the Data

GA4 tables are large. For this workshop we download one week of events (~150,000 rows) once, then save locally to avoid re-querying BigQuery on every render.



Code
```{r}
#| label: download-data
#| eval: false

# ── Run this chunk ONCE. It saves data locally. ───────────────────────────────
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

query_result <- bq_project_query(
  billing_project,
  "SELECT
     event_date,
     event_timestamp,
     event_name,
     event_params,
     user_pseudo_id,
     device,
     geo,
     traffic_source,
     ecommerce,
     items
   FROM `bigquery-public-data.ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce.events_*`
   WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20210101' AND '20210107'" # 90 days of data
)

# A tibble data
ga4_raw <- query_result |>
  bq_table_download(
    bigint = "numeric", # Convert INT64 to R numeric (sufficient for most analyses)
    page_size = 1000 # Download in batches of 10k rows
  )
```








Tip



Since the data is relatively small size, we have three options to save the data as you can see below

RDS,
One Parquet file,
Partitioned Parquet files.




2.2.1 Option 1: Saving it as RDS file


Code
```{r}
#| label: save-rds
#| eval: false
saveRDS(ga4_raw, "data/ga4_raw.rds")
message("Saved ", nrow(ga4_raw), " rows to data/ga4_raw.rds")
```



Note: RDS stands for R Data Serialization



Code
```{r}
#| label: load-rds
#| eval: false

# ── Load from local cache (use this for all subsequent analyses) ──────────────
ga4 <- readRDS("data/ga4_raw.rds")
```




2.2.2 Option 2: Saving as a single Parquet file


Code
```{r}
#| label: save-parquet
#| eval: false

library(arrow)

write_parquet(ga4_raw, "data/ga4_raw.parquet")
message("Saved to data/ga4_raw.parquet")
```




Code
```{r}
#| label: load-parquet
#| eval: false

ga4 <- read_parquet("data/ga4_raw.parquet")
```




2.2.3 Options 3: Saving as Partitioned Parquet

Also no iteration needed — write_dataset() handles the partitioning automatically:



Code
```{r}
#| label: save-partitioned
#| eval: false

library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

ga4_raw |>
  group_by(event_date) |>
  write_dataset("data/ga4_parquet", format = "parquet")

message("Saved partitioned Parquet to data/ga4_parquet/")
```



Note: write_dataset() automatically creates one subfolder per event_date, e.g. data/ga4_parquet/event_date=20210101/part-0.parquet



Code
```{r}
#| label: load-partitioned
#| eval: false

ga4 <- open_dataset("data/ga4_parquet/")
```

3.1 Pattern 1. Query a Parquet file directly with DuckDB (no loading into R)

The most direct approach — point DuckDB at a Parquet file and query it with SQL, no loading required:
DuckDB can scan Parquet files on disk using SQL — nothing enters R memory until you collect().


3.1.1 Simple:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

library(duckdb)
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# Register and query a parquet file directly
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales
  FROM read_parquet('data/sales.parquet')
  GROUP BY region
  ORDER BY total_sales DESC
")
```




3.1.2 Advanced:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

library(duckdb)
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# ── Query a single Parquet file ────────────────────────────────────────────────
dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "
  SELECT
    event_name,
    COUNT(*) AS events,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users
  FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet')
  GROUP BY event_name
  ORDER BY events DESC
  LIMIT 10
"
)

# ── Query multiple Parquet files with a wildcard ───────────────────────────────
# Perfect for GA4's one-file-per-day structure
dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "
  SELECT
    event_date,
    COUNT(*) AS daily_events
  FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_*.parquet')
  GROUP BY event_date
  ORDER BY event_date
"
)

dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "
  SELECT year, SUM(revenue) AS total
  FROM read_parquet('data/sales/*.parquet', union_by_name = TRUE)
  GROUP BY year
  ORDER BY year
"

# ── Join two Parquet files in a single query ───────────────────────────────────
dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "
  SELECT
    s.device_category,
    s.traffic_source_medium,
    COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_pseudo_id) AS users,
    SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchases
  FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet')    AS e
  JOIN read_parquet('data/ga4_sessions.parquet') AS s
    ON e.user_pseudo_id = s.user_pseudo_id
   AND e.event_date     = s.event_date
  GROUP BY s.device_category, s.traffic_source_medium
  ORDER BY users DESC
"
)

dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```



This is powerful — DuckDB pushes the entire query down to the file, reading only the columns and rows it needs (thanks to Parquet’s columnar layout).

3.3 Pattern 3. Query an Arrow Table with DuckDB (The Power Combination)

Arrow and DuckDB are designed to work together. Arrow handles file I/O and in-memory transformation; DuckDB handles querying.
They share data without copying, using the Apache Arrow memory format.
If you already have an Arrow table in memory, DuckDB can query it directly — zero copying involved:


3.3.1 Simple:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)

# Create or load an Arrow table
arrow_table <- read_parquet("data/sales.parquet", as_data_frame = FALSE)

con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
duckdb_register_arrow(con, "sales_arrow", arrow_table)

tbl(con, "sales_arrow") |>
  filter(category == "Electronics") |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price)) |>
  collect()
```




3.3.2 Advanced:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

library(arrow)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)

# ── Step 1: Open Parquet as Arrow Dataset (lazy — nothing loaded yet) ──────────
ga4_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")

# ── Step 2: Do transformations in Arrow ───────────────────────────────────────
# Arrow is better at: filtering rows, selecting columns, type conversion
ga4_prepared <- ga4_arrow |>
  filter(event_name %in% c("purchase", "add_to_cart", "view_item")) |>
  select(event_date, event_name, user_pseudo_id) |>
  mutate(event_date = as.Date(event_date))

# ── Step 3: Hand off to DuckDB for aggregation ────────────────────────────────
# DuckDB is better at: GROUP BY, window functions, complex joins
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# Register the Arrow object directly — ZERO data copying
duckdb_register_arrow(con, "ga4_prepared", ga4_prepared)

# Now query it with full DuckDB SQL power
result <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    event_date,
    event_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users
  FROM ga4_prepared
  GROUP BY event_date, event_name
  ORDER BY event_date, event_name
")

print(result)
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

# ── The same workflow using dplyr throughout ───────────────────────────────────
library(arrow)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)

con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())

# Arrow dataset → register with DuckDB → query with dplyr
ga4_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")
duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "ga4_events", ga4_arrow)

ga4_params_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_event_params.parquet")
duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "ga4_params", ga4_params_arrow)

# Now use pure dplyr — no SQL needed at all
# dbplyr translates these verbs to DuckDB SQL automatically

# Marketing analysis: page views by device and channel
page_analysis <- tbl(con, "ga4_params") |>
  filter(key == "page_location") |>
  rename(page_location = param_value) |>
  left_join(
    tbl(con, "ga4_events") |>
      select(event_timestamp, user_pseudo_id,
             device_category, traffic_source_medium),
    by = c("event_timestamp", "user_pseudo_id")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    page_path = regexp_replace(page_location, "\\?.*$", ""),
    page_path = regexp_replace(page_path, "https?://[^/]+", "")
  ) |>
  group_by(device_category, page_path) |>
  summarise(
    page_views = n(),
    users      = n_distinct(user_pseudo_id),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(page_views >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(page_views)) |>
  head(20) |>
  collect()

print(page_analysis)
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

text:
3.4 Pattern 4. Persistent DuckDB Database (Best for a Course Project)

Write your rectangled GA4 tables once into a .duckdb file. Every subsequent analysis opens this one file — no BigQuery, no Parquet management, no RAM issues:



Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)
library(arrow)

# ── SETUP: Run once to create the database ────────────────────────────────────
con <- dbConnect(
  duckdb::duckdb(),
  dbdir     = "data/ga4.duckdb",
  read_only = FALSE
)

# Write tables from Parquet files — DuckDB reads and stores them
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE ga4_events AS
  SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet')
")

dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE ga4_params AS
  SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_event_params.parquet')
")

dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE ga4_sessions AS
  SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_sessions.parquet')
")

dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE ga4_items AS
  SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_items.parquet')
")

# Add indexes for faster querying
dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_event_name ON ga4_events(event_name)")
dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_param_key  ON ga4_params(key)")
dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_event_date ON ga4_events(event_date)")

# Confirm what was saved
cat("Tables in ga4.duckdb:\n")
dbListTables(con) |> print()

cat("\nRow counts:\n")
purrr::map_df(dbListTables(con), \(t) {
  tibble::tibble(
    table = t,
    rows  = dbGetQuery(con,
              glue::glue("SELECT COUNT(*) n FROM {t}"))$n
  )
}) |> print()

cat("\nFile size:",
    round(file.size("data/ga4.duckdb") / 1024^2, 1), "MB\n")

dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```




Code
```{r}
#| eval: false

# ── ANALYSIS: Open the database for every subsequent session ──────────────────
con <- dbConnect(
  duckdb::duckdb(),
  dbdir     = "data/ga4.duckdb",
  read_only = TRUE    # Prevents accidental writes during analysis
)

# Lazy table references — nothing in RAM yet
events   <- tbl(con, "ga4_events")
params   <- tbl(con, "ga4_params")
sessions <- tbl(con, "ga4_sessions")
items    <- tbl(con, "ga4_items")

# ── Example 1: Event counts (dplyr) ───────────────────────────────────────────
events |>
  count(event_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  collect()

# ── Example 2: Top pages (dplyr) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
params |>
  filter(key == "page_location") |>
  count(param_value, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10) |>
  collect()

# ── Example 3: Revenue by day (SQL) ───────────────────────────────────────────
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    event_date,
    COUNT(*)                                   AS transactions,
    SUM(ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd)     AS revenue,
    AVG(ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd)     AS avg_order_value
  FROM ga4_events
  WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY event_date
  ORDER BY event_date
")

# ── Example 4: Funnel analysis (SQL window functions) ─────────────────────────
dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH funnel AS (
    SELECT
      event_name,
      COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        ORDER BY CASE event_name
          WHEN 'view_item'       THEN 1
          WHEN 'add_to_cart'     THEN 2
          WHEN 'begin_checkout'  THEN 3
          WHEN 'purchase'        THEN 4
        END
      ) AS stage_order
    FROM ga4_events
    WHERE event_name IN ('view_item','add_to_cart',
                         'begin_checkout','purchase')
    GROUP BY event_name
  )
  SELECT
    event_name,
    users,
    ROUND(100.0 * users /
      FIRST_VALUE(users) OVER (ORDER BY stage_order), 1) AS pct_of_top
  FROM funnel
  ORDER BY stage_order
")

dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

6.1 The core difference

open_dataset() is for many files or a folder — it creates a lazy connection without loading anything into memory. read_parquet() is for a single file — it reads the file directly, by default into R memory.
The One-Sentence Description:

```{r}
# read_parquet()  — loads data INTO RAM immediately, gives you a tibble
# open_dataset()  — creates a POINTER to data on disk, loads nothing yet
```
> Everything else flows from this single difference. > > What Each Function Actually Does:

text:
6.2 read_parquet() — Eager Loading


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)

# read_parquet() works like read.csv() or readRDS()
# It reads the file immediately and returns a tibble in memory

ga4_data <- arrow::read_parquet("data/ga4_flat.parquet")

# After this line:
# ✓ All data is in RAM
# ✓ ga4_data is a regular tibble
# ✓ You can use it without Arrow at all — it's just a data frame
# ✗ If the file is larger than RAM — this fails or crashes R

class(ga4_data)
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
# ← a regular tibble, no Arrow in sight after loading

object.size(ga4_data) |> format(units = "MB")
#> "187.4 MB"   ← sitting in your RAM right now
```

text:
6.3 open_dataset() — Lazy Loading


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)

# open_dataset() works like a database connection
# It reads the file METADATA only and returns an Arrow Dataset object
# No actual data rows are loaded until you explicitly ask for them

ga4_dataset <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")

# After this line:
# ✓ Metadata is read (schema, number of rows, column types)
# ✓ You can query it immediately with dplyr verbs
# ✓ Works on files larger than RAM
# ✗ ga4_dataset is NOT a tibble — it is an Arrow Dataset object

class(ga4_dataset)
#> [1] "FileSystemDataset" "Dataset" "ArrowObject" "R6"

#> "4.2 KB"    ← almost nothing in RAM — just the metadata pointer
```

text:
6.4 Side-by-Side Comparison


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# ── Same question asked both ways ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# "What are the top 5 event types by count?"

# ── read_parquet() approach ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Step 1: Load EVERYTHING into RAM (even columns we don't need)
ga4_tibble <- read_parquet("data/ga4_flat.parquet")
# Step 2: Then filter in R
ga4_tibble |>
  count(event_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

# ── open_dataset() approach ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Step 1: Open a pointer (nothing loaded)
ga4_ds <- open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")
# Step 2: Build a query (still nothing loaded)
query <- ga4_ds |>
  count(event_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
# Step 3: Execute — Arrow reads ONLY the event_name column
query |> collect()

# Both produce identical results
# But open_dataset() used a fraction of the RAM
```

text:
6.5 The Key Concept: Lazy vs Eager Evaluation


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

ga4_ds <- open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")

# ── Every dplyr verb on an Arrow Dataset is LAZY ─────────────────────────────
# Nothing happens when you call these — they just build a query plan

step1 <- ga4_ds |> filter(event_name == "purchase")
step2 <- step1  |> select(event_date, user_pseudo_id,
                            ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd)
step3 <- step2  |> group_by(event_date)
step4 <- step3  |> summarise(revenue = sum(ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd,
                                            na.rm = TRUE))

# At this point: ZERO rows have been read from disk
# step4 is just a description of what to do

# ── collect() EXECUTES the query ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Only now does Arrow read from disk — and only the columns it needs
result <- step4 |> collect()

# Arrow read: event_name, event_date, user_pseudo_id,
#             ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd
# Arrow skipped: every other column in the file
# This is called "column pruning" — a massive RAM saving

# ── You can inspect the query plan before executing ───────────────────────────
ga4_ds |>
  filter(event_name == "purchase") |>
  group_by(event_date) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd,
                          na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  explain()    # Shows Arrow's execution plan — no data read yet
```

title: DuckDB for Marketing Analytics: From Parquet to Powerful Queries
text:
6.6 The Biggest Difference: Multiple Files
This is where open_dataset() becomes dramatically more powerful. read_parquet() reads one file. open_dataset() reads many files as if they were one:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)

# ── Scenario: GA4 data saved as one Parquet file per day ─────────────────────
# data/
#   ga4_20201101.parquet
#   ga4_20201102.parquet
#   ga4_20201103.parquet
#   ... (365 files)

# ── read_parquet(): must read files one at a time ─────────────────────────────
library(purrr)

# Cumbersome — load all files and bind them
all_files <- list.files("data", pattern = "ga4_\\d{8}.parquet",
                         full.names = TRUE)

ga4_all <- all_files |>
  map(\(f) read_parquet(f)) |>
  list_rbind()
# Loads ALL files into RAM simultaneously
# If 365 files × 50 MB each = 18 GB — crashes R

# ── open_dataset(): treats ALL files as one dataset ──────────────────────────
ga4_all <- open_dataset("data/")   # Point at the folder, not a file
# OR be more specific:
ga4_all <- open_dataset(
  sources = list.files("data", pattern = "ga4_\\d{8}.parquet",
                        full.names = TRUE)
)

# Now query across ALL 365 days as if it were one table
# Arrow reads only the files and columns needed to answer your query
ga4_all |>
  filter(event_date >= "2021-01-01",
         event_date <= "2021-01-31") |>
  count(event_name) |>
  collect()
# Arrow only opens January files — skips the other 334 files entirely
```

text:
6.7 Hive-Partitioned Datasets — The Most Powerful Pattern


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# ── Save GA4 data in Hive partition format ────────────────────────────────────
# Hive partitioning stores data in folders named key=value
# This lets open_dataset() skip entire folders based on filter conditions

ga4_tibble <- readRDS("data/ga4_raw.rds") |>
  mutate(
    year  = lubridate::year(lubridate::ymd(event_date)),
    month = lubridate::month(lubridate::ymd(event_date))
  )

# Write partitioned dataset
arrow::write_dataset(
  ga4_tibble,
  path             = "data/ga4_partitioned",
  format           = "parquet",
  partitioning     = c("year", "month"),   # Partition by year and month
  compression      = "snappy"
)

# Creates this folder structure:
# data/ga4_partitioned/
#   year=2020/
#     month=11/
#       part-0.parquet
#     month=12/
#       part-0.parquet
#   year=2021/
#     month=1/
#       part-0.parquet
#     month=2/
#       part-0.parquet

# ── open_dataset() understands Hive partitioning automatically ────────────────
ga4_partitioned <- open_dataset(
  "data/ga4_partitioned",
  partitioning = c("year", "month")   # Tell Arrow how it is partitioned
)

# Query January 2021 — Arrow reads ONLY year=2021/month=1/ folder
jan_2021 <- ga4_partitioned |>
  filter(year == 2021, month == 1) |>
  count(event_name) |>
  collect()

# Arrow skipped every other year= and month= folder
# This is called "partition pruning" — can be 100x faster on large datasets

# ── Verify the schema includes partition columns ──────────────────────────────
ga4_partitioned$schema
#> Schema
#> event_date: string
#> event_name: string
#> user_pseudo_id: string
```

6.10 Practical GA4 Workflows

6.10.1 Workflow 1: read_parquet() for Quick Exploration


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# You just created a small processed file and want to inspect it
# File is 15 MB — perfectly fine to load into RAM

ga4_items <- read_parquet("data/ga4_items.parquet")

# Now it is just a tibble — use any R function freely
summary(ga4_items$price_in_usd)
hist(ga4_items$quantity)
View(ga4_items)

# No collect() needed anywhere
ga4_items |>
  filter(item_category == "Apparel") |>
  arrange(desc(price_in_usd)) |>
  head(10)
```




6.10.2 Workflow 2: open_dataset() for Large Event Params


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# event_params unrolled is very large — open_dataset is safer
ga4_params <- open_dataset("data/ga4_event_params.parquet")

# Check size without loading
ga4_params$schema          # Column names and types
nrow(ga4_params)           # Row count — reads metadata only, instant

# Query only what you need — Arrow loads only 2 columns from disk
page_views <- ga4_params |>
  filter(
    event_name  == "page_view",
    key         == "page_location"
  ) |>
  select(event_date, user_pseudo_id, param_value) |>
  collect()   # Only now does data enter RAM — just the filtered subset

nrow(page_views)   # Much smaller than the full params file
```




6.10.3 Workflow 3: open_dataset() Across All GA4 Daily Files


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# GA4 exports one file per day — open_dataset handles all of them
# Save each day as its own Parquet file first:

# data/ga4_daily/
#   ga4_20201101.parquet
#   ga4_20201102.parquet
#   ... etc

# Open all daily files as one unified dataset
ga4_all <- open_dataset(
  sources = list.files(
    "data/ga4_daily",
    pattern    = "\\.parquet$",
    full.names = TRUE
  )
)

cat("Total rows across all files:", nrow(ga4_all), "\n")
cat("Schema:\n")
print(ga4_all$schema)

# Query across the full date range — Arrow only reads what is needed
monthly_summary <- ga4_all |>
  mutate(
    event_date = as.Date(event_date),
    month      = floor_date(event_date, "month")
  ) |>
  group_by(month, event_name) |>
  summarise(
    events = n(),
    users  = n_distinct(user_pseudo_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  collect()

monthly_summary |>
  filter(event_name %in% c("page_view", "purchase",
                             "add_to_cart")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month, y = events,
                  colour = event_name,
                  group  = event_name)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title  = "Monthly Event Trends",
    x      = NULL,
    y      = "Events",
    colour = "Event Type"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```




6.10.4 Workflow 4: Combining Both in One Pipeline


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# Common pattern: open_dataset for the large file, read_parquet for small ones
# Then join them

# Large file — use open_dataset (lazy)
ga4_params <- open_dataset("data/ga4_event_params.parquet")

# Small lookup file — use read_parquet (eager, it's tiny)
page_categories <- read_parquet("data/page_categories.parquet")
# This is a small reference table: page_path → category
# Fine to have in RAM as a regular tibble

# Extract page locations from the large params file lazily
page_data <- ga4_params |>
  filter(key == "page_location") |>
  select(event_date, user_pseudo_id, param_value) |>
  rename(page_url = param_value) |>
  mutate(
    page_path = arrow_string_replace_regex(
      page_url,
      "^https?://[^/]+|\\?.*$", ""
    )
  ) |>
  collect()   # Now bring into RAM — filtered to just page views

# Join with the small lookup table (both in RAM now)
page_data |>
  left_join(page_categories, by = "page_path") |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE)
```




6.10.5 Workflow 5: open_dataset() with DuckDB — The Full Stack


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(arrow)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)

# open_dataset creates Arrow Dataset objects
# DuckDB can query Arrow objects directly — zero data copying

ga4_events_ds <- open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet")
ga4_params_ds <- open_dataset("data/ga4_event_params.parquet")

# Register Arrow datasets with DuckDB
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "events", ga4_events_ds)
duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "params", ga4_params_ds)

# Now use DuckDB SQL on top of Arrow Datasets
# Data stays in Arrow format — no copying between systems
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    e.event_date,
    e.device_category,
    COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_pseudo_id)           AS users,
    SUM(e.ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd)   AS revenue
  FROM events e
  WHERE e.event_name = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY e.event_date, e.device_category
  ORDER BY e.event_date, revenue DESC
")

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

6.11 Which to use for GA4 data?
```{r}
# Ask these questions in order:

# 1. How big is the file?
#    < 500 MB and fits in RAM  → read_parquet() is fine
#    > 500 MB or close to RAM  → open_dataset()

# 2. How many files?
#    One file                  → either works
#    Multiple files or folder  → open_dataset() only

# 3. How many columns do you need?
#    Most or all columns       → read_parquet() is simpler
#    Only a few columns        → open_dataset() (column pruning saves RAM)

# 4. Are you exploring or producing?
#    Exploring unknown data    → read_parquet() (View(), summary(), hist())
#    Building analysis pipeline → open_dataset() (lazy, memory-efficient)

# 5. Do you need the result as a tibble immediately?
#    Yes                       → read_parquet()
#    No — you will filter first → open_dataset() + collect()
```

NoteWhat Does bq_auth() Do?



bq_auth() handles the OAuth2 authentication handshake between R and Google. It opens your browser, asks you to grant R permission to access your Google Cloud account, and then caches the resulting token locally. On subsequent R sessions, the cached token is used automatically — you will only see the browser prompt on your first run.




2.2 Establish the Connection

```{r}

#| eval: true

# ── Connect to the public GA4 dataset ─────────────────────────────────────────
# project  = where the PUBLIC data lives (always "bigquery-public-data")
# dataset  = the specific GA4 dataset name (must be exact — case sensitive)
# billing  = YOUR project (this is what gets charged for query processing)

con <- dbConnect(
  bigrquery::bigquery(),
  project = "bigquery-public-data",
  dataset = "ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce",
  billing = BILLING_PROJECT,
  bigint = "numeric" # Enforces safe conversion of 64-bit timestamps
)

# ── Verify the connection ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
available_tables <- dbListTables(con)

cli::cli_alert_success(
  "Connected. {.val {length(available_tables)}} tables available."
)
cli::cli_alert_info(
  "Date range: {.val {head(available_tables, 1)}} to
  {.val {tail(available_tables, 1)}}"
)
```







NoteAbout the Public Dataset



The dataset ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce is provided by Google and contains real event data from the Google Merchandise Store — an actual e-commerce site selling Google-branded products. User identifiers have been obfuscated for privacy. The data covers November 2020 through January 2022, stored as one BigQuery table per day in the format events_YYYYMMDD.

6 Download: Day-by-Day Loop
This is the main download process. Each iteration:

Checks if the files already exist (skips if so — safe to re-run)
Downloads one day’s data from BigQuery
Saves the raw nested data as .rds
Flattens struct columns and saves as Parquet
Flattens event_params and saves as Parquet
Flattens items and saves as Parquet
Logs the result for the summary report


```{r}
#| label: download-method-update
#| eval: false
library(bigrquery)
library(bigrquerystorage) # Activates BigQuery Storage API streaming

# Inside the loop:
raw_day <- tbl(con, tbl_name) |> collect() # page_size removed entirely
```







WarningDo Not Interrupt This Process



Each day’s files are saved immediately after downloading. If you must stop, simply close R and re-run the chunk later — already-downloaded files are detected and skipped automatically.



```{r}
#| label: download-loop
#| eval: false
#| cache: true

cli::cli_h1("Starting GA4 Download")
cli::cli_alert_info(
  "Downloading {length(target_tables)} tables. Please wait..."
)
cat("\n")

# ── Initialise the download log ────────────────────────────────────────────────
download_log <- vector("list", length(target_tables))
names(download_log) <- target_tables

# ── Main loop ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for (i in seq_along(target_tables)) {
  tbl_name <- target_tables[i]
  date_str <- str_extract(tbl_name, "\\d{8}")

  # File paths for each format
  rds_path <- glue("data/ga4_raw/ga4_{date_str}.rds")
  parq_path <- glue("data/ga4_parquet/ga4_{date_str}.parquet")
  params_path <- glue("data/ga4_parquet_params/params_{date_str}.parquet")
  items_path <- glue("data/ga4_parquet_items/items_{date_str}.parquet")

  all_exist <- all(
    fs::file_exists(rds_path),
    fs::file_exists(parq_path),
    fs::file_exists(params_path)
  )

  # ── Skip if already downloaded ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  if (all_exist) {
    cli::cli_alert_info(
      "[{i}/{length(target_tables)}] Skipping {date_str} — already exists"
    )
    download_log[[tbl_name]] <- list(status = "skipped", rows = NA_integer_)
    next
  }

  # ── Download with error handling ───────────────────────────────────────────
  cli::cli_progress_step(
    "[{i}/{length(target_tables)}] Downloading {date_str}..."
  )

  day_result <- tryCatch(
    {
      # ── Download raw data ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      raw_day <- tbl(con, tbl_name) |> collect()
      n_rows <- nrow(raw_day)

      # ── Save raw nested data as .rds ─────────────────────────────────────────
      # compress = FALSE: fastest read/write — use "gz" to save disk space
      saveRDS(raw_day, rds_path, compress = FALSE)

      # ── Flatten structs and save as Parquet ──────────────────────────────────
      flat_day <- flatten_structs(raw_day)
      write_parquet(flat_day, parq_path, compression = "snappy")

      # ── Flatten event_params and save as Parquet ─────────────────────────────
      params_flat <- flatten_event_params(raw_day)
      if (!is.null(params_flat) && nrow(params_flat) > 0) {
        write_parquet(params_flat, params_path, compression = "snappy")
      }

      # ── Flatten items and save as Parquet ────────────────────────────────────
      items_flat <- flatten_items(raw_day)
      if (!is.null(items_flat) && nrow(items_flat) > 0) {
        write_parquet(items_flat, items_path, compression = "snappy")
      }

      # ── Clean up to free RAM before next iteration ───────────────────────────
      rm(raw_day, flat_day, params_flat, items_flat) # remove
      gc(full = TRUE, verbose = FALSE) # verbose = FALSE argument just suppresses the printed summary that gc() would normally output

      cli::cli_alert_success(
        "  Done: {scales::comma(n_rows)} rows saved in 3 formats"
      )

      list(status = "success", rows = n_rows)
    },
    error = function(e) {
      cli::cli_alert_danger(
        "  FAILED: {date_str} — {conditionMessage(e)}"
      )
      list(status = "error", error = conditionMessage(e), rows = NA_integer_)
    }
  )

  download_log[[tbl_name]] <- day_result

  # ── Brief pause every 10 downloads to avoid rate limiting ─────────────────
  if (i %% 10 == 0 && i < length(target_tables)) {
    cli::cli_alert_info("  Pausing briefly to avoid rate limits...")
    Sys.sleep(3)
  }
}

cli::cli_alert_success("Download loop complete!")
```

11 How to Load Data in Future Sessions






TipQuick Reference — Copy This Into Every Future Notebook



Paste this code block at the top of each subsequent notebook to load all three datasets:
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

ga4_events <- open_dataset("data/ga4_partitioned")
ga4_params <- open_dataset("data/ga4_params_partitioned")
ga4_items  <- open_dataset("data/ga4_items_partitioned")
That is all you need. No BigQuery, no authentication, no waiting.



11.1 The Five Loading Patterns

```{r}
#| label: loading-patterns
#| eval: true
#| cache: false

library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(duckdb)
library(duckplyr)

# ── Pattern 1: Partitioned dataset — recommended for most analyses ─────────────
# Lazy: nothing loaded into RAM until collect()
# Fast: Arrow skips irrelevant year/month folders automatically
ga4_events <- open_dataset("data/ga4_partitioned")
ga4_params <- open_dataset("data/ga4_params_partitioned")
ga4_items <- open_dataset("data/ga4_items_partitioned")

# Query a specific month
november_events <- ga4_events |>
  filter(year == 2020, month == 11) |>
  select(event_date, event_name, user_pseudo_id, device_category) |>
  collect()

# ── Pattern 2: Single day flat Parquet ────────────────────────────────────────
# Eager: loads immediately into RAM as a tibble
# Use for: single-day analysis, quick exploration
day_data <- read_parquet("data/ga4_parquet/ga4_20201101.parquet")
glimpse(day_data) # No list-columns — ready for analysis without further processing

# ── Pattern 3: Raw nested .rds ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Use for: teaching and practising rectangling techniques
raw_day <- readRDS("data/ga4_raw/ga4_20201101.rds")
glimpse(raw_day) # List-columns are still nested — ready for rectangling

# ── Pattern 4: DuckDB on partitioned Parquet ──────────────────────────────────
# Use for: SQL queries, window functions, complex multi-table joins
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
duckdb_register_arrow(con, "events", open_dataset("data/ga4_partitioned"))

duckdb_register_arrow(
  con,
  "params",
  open_dataset("data/ga4_params_partitioned")
)
duckdb_register_arrow(con, "items", open_dataset("data/ga4_items_partitioned"))

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "
  SELECT event_name, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM events
  GROUP BY event_name
  ORDER BY n DESC
  LIMIT 10
"
)

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

# ── Pattern 5: duckplyr on Parquet ────────────────────────────────────────────
# Use for: dplyr syntax with DuckDB speed on large data

# read_parquet_duckdb() automatically registers the Parquet files as a DuckDB table and returns a duckplyr tbl that you can manipulate with dplyr syntax. The data is not loaded into RAM until you call collect().

ga4_duck <- duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb("data/ga4_parquet")

ga4_duck |> glimpse()

ga4_duck |>
  count(event_name, sort = FALSE) |> # sort = false to stay in DuckDB
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(10)
```

12 Troubleshooting

```{r}
#| label: troubleshooting
#| eval: false
#| cache: false

# ── Problem 1: "notFound" error ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# Symptom: Error in bq_post(): Request couldn't be served. [notFound]
# Causes and fixes:

# Cause A: BILLING_PROJECT is wrong
cat("Current billing project:", BILLING_PROJECT, "\n")
bq_projects() # Your project MUST appear in this list

# Cause B: BigQuery API not enabled on your project
# Fix: Go to console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/bigquery.googleapis.com
#      select your project and click Enable

# Cause C: Dataset name has a typo
# The correct name is exactly:
# "ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce"
# Check available datasets:
bq_project_datasets("bigquery-public-data") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(dataset, "ga4"))

# ── Problem 2: Integer overflow warning ───────────────────────────────────────
# Symptom: NAs produced by integer overflow
# Cause: event_timestamp is INT64, too large for R's 32-bit integer
# Fix: collect() via tbl() handles this automatically through Arrow
# If using bq_table_download() directly, add: bigint = "numeric"

# ── Problem 3: Download stalls or times out ───────────────────────────────────
# Fix: The loop saves each day before moving to the next
# Simply re-run the download chunk — already-saved files are skipped
already_saved <- fs::dir_ls("data/ga4_parquet") |>
  fs::path_file() |>
  str_extract("\\d{8}") |>
  na.omit()

still_needed <- date_strings[!date_strings %in% already_saved]
cli::cli_alert_info(
  "{length(still_needed)} tables still need downloading"
)

# ── Problem 4: "Cannot allocate vector" — out of memory ──────────────────────
# Cause: One day's data is larger than available RAM
# Fix: Download fewer columns per day
tbl(con, "events_20201101") |>
  select(
    event_date,
    event_timestamp,
    event_name,
    user_pseudo_id,
    device,
    geo,
    traffic_source
  ) |>
  collect() # Excludes event_params and items — much smaller

# ── Problem 5: Parquet write error with list-columns ─────────────────────────
# Symptom: Error writing Parquet — type not supported
# Cause: Trying to write a tibble that still has list-columns
# Fix: The flatten_structs() function removes event_params and items
# before writing. Check that it ran without error.

# ── Problem 6: Partitioned dataset reads wrong columns ───────────────────────
# Symptom: year and month columns show as integers but filtering fails
# Fix: Confirm the partition columns exist in the schema
open_dataset("data/ga4_partitioned")$schema
# year and month should appear as int32 or int64
```

13 Appendix

13.1 cli Package
cli stands for Command Line Interface. It is an R package for printing clean, formatted, and informative messages to the console during long-running tasks like loops and pipelines. It is developed by Posit (the makers of RStudio).
Why Use cli over message() or print()?

```{r}
# ❌ Base R - plain and hard to scan
message("Downloading table 1 of 92")
print("Done: 51941 rows saved")

# ✅ cli - formatted, colored, and easy to scan
cli::cli_alert_info("Downloading table {1} of {92}")
cli::cli_alert_success("Done: {scales::comma(51941)} rows saved")
```

[1] "Done: 51941 rows saved"




13.2 Most Important Functions

13.2.1 1. Status Alerts

```{r}
cli::cli_alert_info("Starting download...") # ℹ blue  - general info
cli::cli_alert_success("Download complete!") # ✔ green - success
cli::cli_alert_warning("Token refreshing...") # ! yellow - warning
cli::cli_alert_danger("Download failed!") # ✖ red   - error
```



13.2.2 2. Section Headers

```{r}
cli::cli_h1("GA4 Download Pipeline") # Large header
cli::cli_h2("Processing event_params") # Medium header
cli::cli_h3("Flattening structs") # Small header
```



13.2.3 3. Progress Bar for Loops

```{r}
pb <- cli::cli_progress_bar(
  total = 92,
  format = "Downloading {cli::pb_current}/{cli::pb_total} | {cli::pb_bar} | ETA: {cli::pb_eta}"
)

for (i in 1:92) {
  # your download code
  cli::cli_progress_update(id = pb)
}

cli::cli_progress_done(id = pb)
```



13.2.4 4. String Interpolation with {}

```{r}
date <- "20201101"
rows <- 51941

# cli automatically evaluates {} expressions
cli::cli_alert_success("Downloaded {date}: {scales::comma(rows)} rows")
# ✔ Downloaded 20201101: 51,941 rows
```
